newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak referendums end in chaos, boycotted by many.
newsitem.headline: Slovak referendums end in chaos, boycotted by many.

text.p: Polls closed in Slovakia on Saturday on chaotic referendums boycotted by many voters and dismissed by foreign diplomats as a failed test of the former communist country's commitment to democracy.
Many polling stations reported a turnout of no more than 10 percent.
An feud between the president and prime minister erupted into the open after a question on whether the public should elect the president was taken off ballot papers at the last minute.
The remaining questions on the ballot dealt only with whether Slovaks support NATO membership, now almost an irrelevant issue.

"After this, it's out of the question that Slovakia will be invited to join NATO in the first round of enlargement," said President Michal Kovac, who himself boycotted the poll because the question on how his successor will be chosen was missing.

A proposal to have the next president elected directly instead of by parliament had been framed for the voters by those who want to prevent Kovac's rival, Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, from inheriting presidential powers when Kovac's term ends next March.
The question was struck off at the last moment by Meciar's Interior Minister Gustav Krajci, despite a Central Referendum Committee (UKR) ruling that it should be included.

Results from the two-day poll will be announced on Sunday afternoon. But as polls closed, a senior UKR official said the committee had received 150 official complaints from all over Slovakia, and that it would launch a legal action against Krajci for spoiling the referendum.
"The minister... was probably thwarting the referendum by not providing the valid ballot papers," said Jozef Krumpolec, UKR vice-chairman.
Mayors in many towns had refused to accept the ballot papers bearing only the three questions on NATO, sent out on Friday. Where voters were offered them, many refused to vote.

In Kosice, Slovakia's second city and once a Meciar stronghold, protests and apathy kept all but a trickle of voters away from the polls. Mayor Rudolf Schuster, a possible presidential candidate, joined the boycott.

"We found ourself legally obliged to offer the citizens ballots with only three questions, but we will not endorse the vote at the end," a member of the local referendum commitee in one Bratislava district told Reuters.
He said that, with an hour to go before polls closed, less than 10 percent of voters had cast their ballots there. Many looked at the three-question voting slip and walked out.
The Slovakian news agency TASR reported a similar picture nationwide.
Western diplomats had rated the plebiscite as a key test of the Meciar government's commitment to democracy.

The government's official stance is that Slovakia, formed when Czechoslovakia split in 1993, wants to be among the first new members of NATO. But its chances have waned after Western criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
"The referendum has already been totally discredited and will have no legal significance. This is tragic," one envoy in Bratislava said on Friday.
The dispute over the presidential elections springs from a clause in the constitution requiring a three-fifths majority in parliament to elect the president.

If no candidates can muster a sufficient margin -- as seems likely given the present strengths of the parties -- presidential powers would pass to the prime minister, a provision the present prime minister has fought to keep.
